I.explanation: "I" means "you" when you talk to a group of people (more than one). It is not the English "I", which is "jeg". Use "du" (you, one person) for one person and "I" for a group. Do not mix it up with small "i", which means "in".

related.en: you (group), as in "Jeg ser jer" (I see you)

sentence.en: Where are you all going this weekend?

at invitere.explanation: "At invitere" means "to invite". "Jeg inviterer dig til min fødselsdag" means "I invite you to my birthday". "Til" (to) goes before the event you invite someone to. "En invitation" means "an invitation".

sentence.en: I invite you to my birthday.

en idé.explanation: "En idé" means "an idea", and it is spelled with an accent on the e. Two phrases you will often hear are "Det er en god idé" (That is a good idea) and "Jeg har ingen idé" (I have no idea).

en indkøbskurv.explanation: "En indkøbskurv" means "a shopping basket", the kind you carry by hand in a shop. A bigger one on wheels is "en indkøbsvogn" (a shopping cart). The word is built from "indkøb" (shopping) and "en kurv" (a basket).

sentence.en: I am taking a shopping basket.

en indkøbspose.explanation: "En indkøbspose" means "a shopping bag", the bag you carry your groceries in. It is built from "indkøb" (shopping) and "en pose" (a bag), and in everyday talk Danes often just say "en pose".

sentence.en: I have forgotten my shopping bag.

en indkøbsvogn.explanation: "En indkøbsvogn" means "a shopping cart", the kind on wheels that you push around a supermarket. It is built from "indkøb" (shopping) and "en vogn" (a cart).

sentence.da: Du skal bruge en mønt til **indkøbsvognen**.
sentence.en: You need a coin for the shopping cart.

et indkøbscenter.explanation: "Et indkøbscenter" means "a shopping mall", a large building with many shops. It is made of "indkøb" (shopping) and "et center" (a center).

sentence.en: We are meeting at the shopping mall.

i.explanation: "I" means "in". It is used for places ("i Danmark", in Denmark), months ("i juni", in June) and how long something lasts ("i to timer", for two hours). Do not mix it up with "på" (on, at), which Danes use for islands: "på Fyn" (on Funen).

forms.en: What are you doing this evening?

i aften.explanation: "I aften" means "this evening", the evening of today that is still to come. Danes say it a lot when making plans. For the evening that has already passed, use "i aftes" (last night).

sentence.da: Vi skal spise middag sammen **i aften**.
sentence.en: We are having dinner together this evening.

forms.en: I was at home last night.

i aftes.explanation: "I aftes" means "last night", the evening that has just passed (yesterday evening). Do not mix it up with "i aften" (this evening, still to come). For the sleeping hours, "i nat" (last night) is more common.

sentence.en: I watched a movie last night.

i dag.explanation: "I dag" means "today" and is written as two words: "I dag regner det" (It is raining today). Its neighbours are "i går" (yesterday) and "i morgen" (tomorrow). For the evening of today, say "i aften" (this evening).

forms.en: What are you doing this afternoon?

i eftermiddag.explanation: "I eftermiddag" means "this afternoon", the afternoon of today, usually for plans. For something that happens every afternoon, use "om eftermiddagen" (in the afternoons).

forms.en: I was sick the day before yesterday.
It happened the day before yesterday.

i forgårs.explanation: "I forgårs" means "the day before yesterday", two days ago. It is one step further back than "i går" (yesterday). It is the mirror of "i overmorgen" (the day after tomorrow).

sentence.en: We met the day before yesterday.

i går.explanation: "I går" means "yesterday" and is written as two words: "I går regnede det" (It rained yesterday). For yesterday evening you say "i går aftes", and for yesterday morning "i går morges". The opposite is "i morgen" (tomorrow).

sentence.en: We were at the cinema yesterday.

i morgen.explanation: "I morgen" means "tomorrow" and is written as two words. For tomorrow morning you say "i morgen tidlig" (early tomorrow), and for tomorrow evening "i morgen aften". Do not mix it up with "en morgen" (a morning).

forms.da: Jeg stod op tidligt i morges.
forms.en: I got up early this morning.

i morges.explanation: "I morges" means "this morning", but only once the morning is over: "Hun ringede i morges" (She called this morning). For a morning still to come, say "i morgen tidlig" (tomorrow morning).

i nat.explanation: "I nat" can mean "tonight" or "last night". The rest of the sentence tells you which: talking about something that happened means last night, talking about plans means tonight.

forms.da: Er der en butik i nærheden?

i nærheden.explanation: "I nærheden" means "nearby". Add "af" (of) and a place to say near that place: "i nærheden af banegården" (near the train station). It is handy for asking about shops or hotels. The opposite is "langt væk" (far away).

i orden.explanation: "I orden" means "all right" or "in order". "Det er i orden" (That is all right) can answer an apology, like "no problem". "Er alt i orden?" (Is everything all right?) checks that nothing is wrong. It is a bit more formal than "det er fint" (that's fine).

forms.en: See you the day after tomorrow.
I am leaving the day after tomorrow.

i overmorgen.explanation: "I overmorgen" means "the day after tomorrow", two days from now. It is one step further ahead than "i morgen" (tomorrow) and is mostly used for plans. It is the mirror of "i forgårs" (the day before yesterday).

sentence.en: Our guests are coming the day after tomorrow.

i skole.explanation: "I skole" means "in school", as a pupil taking part in lessons. There is no "a" or "the" in it: "Børnene er i skole" (The children are in school). To go there: "Jeg skal i skole" (I am going to school). For the building, say "i skolen" (in the school).

sentence.en: The children are in school now.

i stykker.explanation: "I stykker" means "broken", literally "in pieces". Use it with "er" (is): "Computeren er i stykker" (The computer is broken). It is for things that are physically broken.

i udlandet.explanation: "I udlandet" means "abroad", in another country. Going there is "til udlandet" (to abroad), and coming from there is "fra udlandet" (from abroad). A person from another country is "en udlænding" (a foreigner).

forms.en: What are you doing this weekend?

i weekenden.explanation: "I weekenden" means "this weekend" or "at the weekend". Which weekend you mean depends on the sentence: coming up in "Vi ses i weekenden", already gone in a story about the past. It also covers weekends in general: "Jeg sover længe i weekenden" (I sleep late at the weekend).

sentence.en: I am visiting my family this weekend.

i år.explanation: "I år" means "this year", the one you are in now. For last year say "sidste år", and for next year "næste år".

sentence.en: We are going on vacation this year.

igen.explanation: "Igen" means "again", and also "back": "Jeg kommer igen" can mean "I'll come back" or "I'll come again". Do not mix it up with "også" (also, too).

igennem.explanation: "Igennem" means "through", going from one side of something to the other: "igennem skoven" (through the forest). "Gennem" is a shorter form with the same meaning. It also means "all the way through": "Læs det igennem" (Read it through).

ikke.explanation: "Ikke" means "not". It comes after words like "kan" (can) and "er" (is): "Jeg kan ikke" (I cannot), "Han er ikke her" (He is not here). It does not mean "no": to answer "no", say "nej".

ikke endnu.explanation: "Ikke endnu" means "not yet" and is a handy short answer to "Are you ready?" In a longer sentence "endnu" (yet) usually goes at the end: "Jeg har ikke spist endnu" (I haven't eaten yet). Do not mix it up with "ikke mere" (no more).

ikke mere.explanation: "Ikke mere" means "no more" (you have had enough) or "not anymore" (something has stopped). "Ikke mere, tak" is a polite way to refuse more food or drink. In a longer sentence it often goes at the end: "Hun arbejder her ikke mere" (She does not work here anymore).

sentence.da: Tak for mad, men **ikke mere**, tak.
sentence.en: Thanks for the food, but no more, thank you.

ild.explanation: "Ild" means "fire", as in flames and burning. Do not mix it up with "en brand" (a harmful fire, like a house fire) or "et bål" (a bonfire or campfire). You can say "Der er ild i huset" (the house is on fire) or "Der er brand" (there is a fire).

sentence.en: The children sit around the fire.

imellem.explanation: "Imellem" means "between", as in "Jeg sidder imellem Anna og Peter" (I sit between Anna and Peter). In the phrase "en gang imellem" it means "once in a while". The shorter "mellem" (between) means the same and is more common.

sentence.en: I am sitting between Anna and Peter.

ind.explanation: "Ind" means "in" when something moves from outside to inside, as in "Kom ind!" (Come in!). When someone is already inside, Danes say "inde" (inside, being there) instead. "Ind i" means "into", as in "ind i rummet" (into the room). The opposite of "ind" is "ud" (out).

sentence.en: Would you like to come in?

inden.explanation: "Inden" means "before" and is used when saying what happens first, as in "inden jeg går" (before I go). The word "før" (before) means almost the same and is also common. "Inden for" means "within", as in "inden for en time" (within an hour).

indenfor.explanation: "Indenfor" means "inside", and it is also the friendly invitation "Kom indenfor!" (Come on in!). With a time it means "within", as in "indenfor en uge" (within a week). It can also be written as two words, "inden for".

indien.explanation: "Indien" means "India". Notice the spelling: it ends in "-ien", not "-ia". A person from India is "en inder" (an Indian), and "indisk" means "Indian", as in "indisk mad" (Indian food).

indisk.explanation: "Indisk" means "Indian", as in from India, and is often used about food. It is written with a small letter, unlike "Indian" in English. Do not mix it up with "indianer" (a Native American).

sentence.en: We are ordering Indian food today.

indtil.explanation: "Indtil" means "until" and marks the point when something stops. It works with a time ("indtil klokken fem", until five o'clock) and with a whole sentence ("indtil du kommer", until you come). "Indtil videre" is a common way to say "for now" or "until further notice".

influenza.explanation: "Influenza" means "the flu", a stronger illness than a cold, often with fever and body aches. You say "Jeg har influenza" (I have the flu), usually without "en" (a) in front.

sentence.da: Jeg har **influenza** og skal blive hjemme.
sentence.en: I have the flu and have to stay home.

ingen.explanation: "Ingen" means "no one" or "none", and also "no" in front of a thing, as in "ingen penge" (no money). It already carries the "not", so you do not add "ikke" (not). For "nothing" use "ingenting".

ingen problemer.explanation: "Ingen problemer" means "no problem" and is a relaxed answer to thanks or to a request. A longer way to say it is "det er ikke noget problem" (it is not a problem). It sounds casual and friendly, like in English.

sentence.en: Can you help me? — No problem.

forms.en: Thanks for the help. Don't mention it.

forms.da: Ingen årsag, det var så lidt.

ingen årsag.explanation: "Ingen årsag" literally means "no reason" and is a reply to thanks, like "don't mention it". Other replies to thanks are "selv tak" (you're welcome) and "det var så lidt" (it was nothing).

sentence.en: Thanks a lot! — Don't mention it.

ingenting.explanation: "Ingenting" means "nothing". It is built from "ingen" (no) and "ting" (thing). Like "ingen", it already carries the "not", so you do not add "ikke" (not). The opposite is "alt" (everything).

interessant.explanation: "Interessant" means "interesting". The idea of being interested is "at interessere sig for" (to be interested in), as in "Jeg er interesseret i musik" (I am interested in music). The opposite of "interessant" is "kedelig" (boring).

internet.explanation: "Internet" means "internet". Danes say "på internettet" (on the internet), and they also often use the English word "online", as in "Jeg er online" (I am online).

is.explanation: "Is" means both "ice cream" and "ice", so the situation shows which one is meant. To order a scoop, you say "en kugle is" (a scoop of ice cream, literally "a ball of ice cream").

sentence.en: The children want ice cream after dinner.

island.explanation: "Island" means "Iceland". Watch out: it looks like the English word "island", but an island in Danish is "en ø". A person from Iceland is "en islænding" (an Icelander), and "islandsk" means "Icelandic".

isslag.explanation: "Isslag" means "freezing rain", rain that freezes as it hits the ground and makes roads and paths very slippery. It is built from "is" (ice) and "slag" (a blow, a hit). You will see it in winter weather warnings.

sentence.da: Der er varsel om **isslag** i nat.
sentence.en: There is a warning of freezing rain tonight.

italien.explanation: "Italien" means "Italy". Notice the spelling: it ends in "-ien", not "-y". A person from Italy is "en italiener" (an Italian), and "italiensk" means "Italian", as in "italiensk mad" (Italian food).

italiensk.explanation: "Italiensk" means "Italian", for things from Italy and for the language, as in "Jeg taler italiensk" (I speak Italian). It is written with a small letter, unlike "Italian" in English.
